rows.en: These eshkolot ["clusters," that is, the pairs] were Joshua ben Peraḥiah and Nittai the Arbelite; Joshua was Nasi and Nittai Av Beit Din (Ḥagigah 2:2). No halakhot are found in their name except one in the name of Joshua ben Peraḥiah: "Wheat that comes from Alexandria is unclean because of their antlia" (Tosefta Makhshirin ch. 3; R. Samson [of Sens] on the Mishnah there 6:2). For by means of the antlia, which is the bucket with which the Egyptians watered the fields from the waters of the Nile, and because the water was poured with human intent, the wheat became susceptible to impurity (*Erekh Millin*, p. 101). Therefore Joshua ben Peraḥiah was concerned about the wheat that came from there, lest it had become moistened by the water after it was already detached and so had become susceptible to impurity. But the Sages did not agree with him and were not concerned about this; rather they said: "If so, let it be unclean for Joshua ben Peraḥiah (since he is concerned about this, he may be stringent with himself) and clean for all Israel," for we are not concerned lest it became moistened.{v1_07_18:1} And indeed it is very possible that Joshua had a further, hidden intention in this. For although most of the traces that point to the house of Onias and to the opinion of the sages of the Land of Israel about it tell us that they raised no great objection against it and were accommodating toward it, willingly or unwillingly, still we find that this house had some opponents who went so far in their resentment of it that they did not grant it the sanctity of a house of the God of Israel (Menaḥot 109a). Now perhaps Joshua too was in his heart opposed to this house, and devised a remote concern in order to show that all the produce of the land of Egypt is of doubtful impurity, and therefore all their meal offerings that they would offer in the house of Onias are unclean. Apart from this halakhah nothing of his has survived in matters of halakhah, but there is from him a very precious moral saying (Avot 1): "Make for yourself a master and acquire for yourself a companion." In these words there is a warning needed for that time, in which the division of opinions in matters of religion and Torah was growing ever greater; and at such a time it was surely very necessary to rouse the hearts to expound the Torah and to cleave to it according to the views of the Pharisees. This is attained through study with a worthy master and through attachment to companions. These two principles that Joshua set up bear on their face the stamp of his love for the teaching of the Pharisees and of his effort to root it among his people. And he also set up a third principle, whose foundation lies in feelings of love for human beings; he used to say: "Judge every person on the scale of merit." We have no measure of kindness and love toward human beings greater than this. From Nittai the Arbelite too we have received a precious saying (also there), but this sage speaks with a very bitter soul. He used to say: "Keep far from an evil neighbor, do not associate with the wicked, and do not despair of retribution." And there was no time in which the warning against associating with the wicked was more fitting than the time of John Hyrcanus. For John himself, although his hand was with the Pharisees, nevertheless did not keep far from the evil neighbors, who were, in the view of the Pharisees, the Sadducean Jews; he associated with them and dealt with them in brotherhood. It is very likely that when Nittai warned to keep far from the evil neighbor and not to associate with the wicked, the conduct of John was before his eyes. For from a terrible event that happened at the end of John's days it appears that Nittai the Arbelite spoke well and foresaw what was to come.⚠1

rows.en: King Yannai (that is, John the high priest, not Alexander Yannai) went to Koḥalit in the wilderness and conquered sixty towns there, and on his return he rejoiced greatly and called all the sages of Israel. He said to them: "Our fathers ate salted herbs when they were occupied with building the Temple; let us too eat salted herbs in memory of our fathers." And they brought up salted herbs on tables of gold. There was a man there, a scoffer, evil-hearted and worthless, and Eleazar ben Po'irah was his name (according to Josephus, Jonathan the Sadducee), and Eleazar said to Yannai: "King Yannai, the hearts of the Pharisees are against you." "And what shall I do?" "Stand up before them with the frontlet between your eyes." There was an elder there, and Judah ben Gedidim was his name (Josephus calls him Eleazar), and Judah ben Gedidim said to Yannai: "King Yannai, the crown of kingship is enough for you; leave the crown of priesthood to the seed of Aaron," for people said that his mother had been taken captive in Modi'im. The matter was investigated and not found [true], and the sages of Israel departed in anger (their anger was kindled at the words of the elder, who suspected Yannai of being the son of a captive woman without cause, and for this reason they passed sentence of lashes on Judah). And Eleazar ben Po'ira said to King Yannai: "King Yannai, a commoner in Israel, such is his judgment (for if he spreads an evil name about his fellow, his sentence is lashes), and you are king and high priest, is such your judgment? (Does not the strict measure of law dictate that the punishment of one who insults a person grows with the greatness of that person's rank?)" "And what shall I do?" "If you take my advice, trample them." "And the Torah, what will become of it?" "Behold, it is rolled up and lying in a corner; whoever wishes to learn may come and learn." And they killed all the sages of Israel, and the world was desolate until Simeon ben Shetaḥ came and restored the Torah to its former state (Kiddushin 66a).{v1_07_19:1} However, what is told here, that all the sages of Israel were killed, was not so according to the account of Josephus; he only tells that he separated from the Pharisees, abandoned their teaching and joined the Sadducees. This association was the cause that all the laws and statutes deriving from the Oral Torah were abolished. And not only did he abolish them, but he set a punishment on anyone who would follow the Pharisees. Therefore, from the end of John's days until the time of Simeon ben Shetaḥ the hand of the Pharisees was underneath, and the ways of their teaching were in mourning. Without doubt at that time he also removed Joshua ben Peraḥiah from his high office. And perhaps the words of Joshua (Menaḥot 109b) refer to that time: "At first, whoever told me, 'Go up to it' (to office), I would bind him and put him before the lion; now, whoever tells me to go down from it, I would pour a kettle of hot water on him." And it seems that at that time Joshua fled from the wrath of the government and went to Alexandria, where he stayed until the days of wrath were over, when Simeon ben Shetaḥ brought him back, as will be told in the next chapter. Thus this separation, by which John separated from the Pharisees at the end of his days, brought great harm to the exposition of the Torah. He removed the Pharisees even from the Sanhedrin and called Sadducees to their place, and all religious matters were decided by them; and this lasted a long time, for even after John's death the matter did not change. Aristobulus his son, who reigned after him, did not depart from his father's last ways of hating the Pharisees and siding with the Sadducees. This Aristobulus did not reign more than one year. His brother Alexander Yannai came to the throne after him, and he married the widow of Aristobulus, who was his yevamah [his brother's widow]. And although he was high priest, who may not marry a widow even when she is his yevamah (Yevamot 20a), he married her before he was appointed high priest. For when Aristobulus died, Yannai was still in the prison where his brother had shut him up with the rest of his brothers. But at his death the kingdom came into the hands of his wife Shelamzion, and she brought all her husband's brothers out of prison and bound herself to Yannai in the bond of marriage (Josephus, *Antiquities* 13, 11). Now without doubt she made this bond at once, before he was appointed high priest, and in that way a high priest is permitted to marry a widow (Yevamot, there). And perhaps this event was the reason for the sages to establish this halakhah and on its basis to permit Yannai to marry his brother's widow. We do not find that Yannai did harm to the Pharisees at the beginning of his reign. But neither was the Sanhedrin of Sadducees removed at the beginning of his reign, and every dispute and every plague still came before them, as it had from the end of John's days until then.
Simeon ben Shetaḥ; Judah ben Tabbai; the victory of the Pharisees.

Under the rule of Yannai the hand of the Sadducees was still uppermost, and they sat first in the Sanhedrin, for the decree of John had not come to an end and had not been annulled. The Pharisees refrained from sitting with the Sadducees in the Sanhedrin, except for one sage of the Pharisees, who nevertheless made the effort to sit in the Sanhedrin, although he was always forced to set aside his opinion before theirs, for they were the majority. But he did not do this out of love of honor and authority. For a man who sits in a seat among opponents, where none of his words are heeded, where is the honor and where is the authority? Rather, his inner recognition of the justice and truth of the views that he carried in his heart and on his lips did this. He would not tire or weary of opposing them, even if his strength was spent in vain. He saw and knew that their strength would not last forever and that their views had no standing. For the foundations of the views of the Sadducees cannot stand against time and its changes, whereas the views of the Pharisees, together with the ways of midrash of the Pharisees, are fitted to all times with their changes and their demands. Therefore his heart was confident that the days would come when the rule of the Sadducees would be humbled; and with this confidence, how should he bury his hand in the dish [Proverbs 19:24]? This sage was Simeon ben Shetaḥ. He refused to keep away from them and leave them a free hand to do as their heart desired. Rather, he stood against them in open opposition, guided by counsel and knowledge and carried on by compelling proofs and arguments. By these he hoped to overcome them little by little and to push them from their position step by step. Nor was his hope disappointed. Various qualities joined together in him for good and benefit, and they stood by him to make his purpose prosper in his hand. His wisdom and his faith, his uprightness and his righteousness toward God and man, and his calm of spirit in his dispute won him all hearts together; his tongue was choice silver [Proverbs 10:20], knowing how to order his words with judgment, and this gained him the favor of every man and gave him grace when he stood before king and princes. Through these qualities too he was close to the throne, and beloved and favored by Queen Shelamzion (according to some he was her brother (Berakhot 48a)). Not many days passed before he defeated the Sadducees with his proofs. Many of them, who would not bow under the force of his proofs and were powerless to answer them, chose to leave their seat in the Sanhedrin, until they had all separated from the Sanhedrin and Pharisees came in their place, as Simeon had hoped from the start. So it was, and so it was done before the eyes of King Yannai and Queen Shelamzion. For then, when the Sadducees were sitting in their Sanhedrin, King Yannai and Queen Shelamzion, who sat beside him, were sitting at their gathering, and not one of Israel (that is, of the Pharisees) sat with them except Simeon ben Shetaḥ. They would ask for responsa and halakhot and did not know how to bring proof from the Torah. Simeon ben Shetaḥ said to them: "Whoever knows how to bring proof from the Torah shall be fit to sit in the Sanhedrin." Once a practical case arose among them and they did not know how to bring proof from the Torah, except for one elder who babbled against him and said to him: "Give me time." He went and sat by himself, and when he saw that he did not know how to bring proof from the Torah, the next day he was ashamed to come to the Sanhedrin, and Simeon ben Shetaḥ set one of the students in his place. And so he did every single day until they had all withdrawn and the Sanhedrin of Israel sat according to their view; and that day they made a festival. That day was the twenty-eighth of the month of Tevet (Megillat Ta'anit ch. 10). And when Simeon ben Shetaḥ had defeated the Sadducees by his wisdom, he remembered Joshua ben Peraḥiah, who had come down from his office of Nasi and fled to Egypt, and he made haste to call him to Jerusalem. Simeon wrote to the heads of the people in Alexandria in these words: "From Jerusalem the holy city to you, Alexandria my sister: my husband dwells in your midst and I sit desolate" (Bavli Sotah, Amsterdam edition). Because of this call Joshua returned, and without doubt he became Nasi as he had been before, and Simeon ben Shetaḥ was Av Beit Din, for one raises in holiness and does not lower.{v1_08_02:1} At that time too they abolished the book of statutes called *Sefer Gezerta*, which the Sadducees had for capital cases, fines and civil cases. For when the Sadducees stood in the Sanhedrin, the Sadducees had a book of decrees written and laid out: these are stoned, these are burned, these are beheaded, these are strangled; and when they judged a man, they would keep asking and looking in the book. This book they abolished, and that day they made a festival; that day was the fourteenth of the month of Tammuz (Megillat Ta'anit ch. 4). Now we do not know how many years the rule of the Sadducees lasted, for we are told only that they grew strong at the end of John's life, but it is not known how many years before his death this event took place; and the reign of Aristobulus lasted only a little more than one year. When Yannai came to the throne, the matter remained as it had been at the end of John's reign. The wars that he fought and the hardships that passed over him did not allow him to set his eye on religious matters, and therefore Simeon ben Shetaḥ, whom the queen helped, succeeded in removing the Sadducees little by little from the Sanhedrin, until at last they had all been removed and all the members of the Sanhedrin were Pharisees. In any case it appears from all this that days and years passed during which the world was desolate, until Simeon ben Shetaḥ came and removed the Sadducees, until he left them not a single survivor in the Sanhedrin.

footnotes.en: The conclusion of the Gemara in Menaḥot is: "He has fulfilled [his vow] and is liable to karet." This is astonishing: how could it occur to anyone that a man fulfills his obligation with a sacrifice and is liable to karet for offering it? And they said that if he offered it in the house of Onias he has not fulfilled [his vow]; if he were liable to karet, why did they say only "he has not fulfilled"? Should they not have said also "and is liable to karet"? And the baraitot in the Tosefta ch. 12, where it is said explicitly "he has not fulfilled and is liable to karet; he has fulfilled and is liable to karet," are of no use to us, for anyone who has an eye to see will find that these baraitot are not ancient but were founded on the conclusion of the Gemara, as is the case with many baraitot in the Tosefta. This will be clarified further below when we speak of the Tosefta. In the Gemara R. Yoḥanan explained the Mishnah in this direction, and they try to bring proof for R. Yoḥanan's explanation and did not cite the Tosefta; and Rava too tried to reconcile the matter and did not know of the Tosefta. And from [the statement of] Rabbah bar bar Ḥana in the name of R. Yoḥanan, "One who says, 'I take upon myself a burnt offering that I will offer in the house of Onias,' and offered it in the Land of Israel, has fulfilled and is liable to karet," it is proved that if he offered it in the house of Onias he is not liable to karet; for otherwise, why did he not tell us a greater novelty, that even when he offered it in the house of Onias he is liable to karet? Nor is anything proved from the baraita in the Gemara, "I take upon myself a burnt offering that I will offer in the wilderness," and he offered it across the Jordan, "he has fulfilled and is liable to karet"; for this was said only of places where it was not permitted, but in the house of Onias it was permitted for the needs of the hour. And indeed they said explicitly (there, 109b) that they offered burnt offerings on it for the sake of Heaven, and this shows that they gave a justification for the matter and were not concerned about [the prohibition of] slaughtering outside [the Temple]. What the Tosafot wrote, that the altar was for the descendants of Noah, is contrary to the facts. In short, "he has fulfilled and is liable to karet" is only for the sake of dialectic.

R. Zacharias Frankel, in *Darkhei ha-Mishnah*, p. 34, asked: what did the Sages answer him? Was Joshua not to be believed? And how did they decide that it is clean for all Israel? Let them ask those coming from Alexandria whether Joshua's words are correct! He explains that the water drawn by the antlia was at first desired for something attached [to the ground], and of the water much moisture remained and came onto the harvested wheat. Joshua considered that this falls under liquid whose beginning was desired, even though its end was not desired, which is under "if [water] be put" [Leviticus 11:38]; and the Sages disagree, since at the beginning it was for the need of something attached, and it is like "so that the wall may be rinsed" (Makhshirin 4:3). Now if this is by way of dialectic, we accept it; but if as law, there is an answer. For it still needs proof whether water drawn to soften the ground and water it, where one also wants to soften the clods of earth on it, falls under the need of something attached; and we have learned (there 3:4): "One who sprinkles his house and put wheat in it, and it became damp: if from the water, it is under 'if [water] be put.'" Further, if they disagreed on the law, there is a dispute here; why then did they say there was no dispute in Israel? Therefore it is certain that Joshua did not say "certainly unclean," but that there is a concern for impurity, lest they became moistened, as I wrote in the text. And the Sages answered: if he wants to be stringent with himself because of a concern, let him be stringent, but not for others. And there is proof from the Tosefta beside it: "Ḥalafta ben Kuyna says: the garlic of Baal Bekhi is unclean, because they sprinkle it with water and afterward braid it. The Sages said: If so, let it be unclean for Ḥalafta and clean for all Israel." Here the reason of the Sages is without doubt that we are not concerned at all lest water came on it; for if they agreed that water certainly came on it, there would be no doubt that it is unclean according to all. Therefore also in the Tosefta that speaks of Joshua, whose wording and form are exactly like the first, the meaning of the words is without doubt the same. And there, 3:5, we learned: "One who sprinkles his threshing floor need not be concerned lest he put wheat in it and it became damp." Whoever studies this mishnah will find that it is the very law of the Tosefta according to our explanation, and there is no need to go on about this further.

From the wording of this story it appears that it is old but fragmentary. (a) The statement "and the sages of Israel departed in anger" is difficult. For if, as Rashi explains, the king was angry with them, it is not in its place here, but only afterward, when Eleazar incited him against the Pharisees. (b) Judah sinned, and the wrath went out against all the Pharisees? Surely the Pharisees too were angry with Judah, as Josephus tells. (c) The words of Eleazar too are not understood, when he said: "A commoner in Israel, such is his judgment, and you are king and high priest, such is your judgment"; Rashi explains: to bear his insult; but this is not the meaning of the word din. Therefore it seems to me that a whole statement is missing, and the meaning of the words is this: after the matter was investigated and found false, the sages of Israel departed in anger at Judah, as Josephus tells. And after the statement "and the sages of Israel departed in anger" a statement is missing whose content is that they sentenced Judah to lashes, as is also told in Josephus; and on this Eleazar said: "King Yannai, a commoner in Israel, such is his judgment, lashes, for one who spreads an evil name about his fellow; and you are king and high priest: is it not fitting that there be another punishment greater than this?" This agrees with the words of Josephus, who wrote that after they had passed the sentence of lashes, the Sadducee incited John against the Pharisees. From this event it follows for us that lashes for one who spreads an evil name was something the Sadducees agreed with, and necessarily the words "and they shall chastise him" [Deuteronomy 22:18], said of one who spreads an evil name, were understood as lashes, and this was not learned by a gezerah shavah (Ketubbot 46a); and in the Sifrei, Ki Teze, section 238, no gezerah shavah is mentioned. We further learn that in the view of the Sadducees the punishment of one who spreads an evil name follows the rank of the one shamed, while in the view of the Pharisees there is one law for every person. And see what I wrote in the journal *Ha-Shaḥar*, published by R. Peretz Smolenskin, year 2, issue 3.

According to the reading of the Bavli it was Joshua ben Peraḥiah who was in Alexandria and returned at the call of Simeon ben Shetaḥ; according to the reading of Yerushalmi Ḥagigah 2:2 and Sanhedrin 6:6, it was Judah ben Tabbai. Likewise there are two versions concerning Simeon's office of Nasi: according to one reading Simeon was Nasi and Judah ben Tabbai Av Beit Din, and some say the reverse (Bavli Ḥagigah 16a⚠1, and Yerushalmi there). Yet according to the reading of the Bavli in Sanhedrin it is possible to find an explanation of the matter. It is true that Joshua ben Peraḥiah fled from Jerusalem when John persecuted the Pharisees and Joshua was removed from his office of Nasi; he then went to Alexandria and stayed there until Simeon succeeded in overcoming the Sadducees. At that time Simeon wrote to Alexandria and brought Joshua ben Peraḥiah back to be Nasi as before his flight, with Simeon as Av Beit Din. And necessarily it was so, if we assume that Simeon's victory over the Sadducees was in Yannai's lifetime and that it was at that time that Simeon wrote to Alexandria; and it is not possible that this letter refers to anyone other than Joshua ben Peraḥiah. For until that time when Simeon came and brought back the Pharisees, the world was surely desolate (Kiddushin 66a); therefore it is certain that from the days of John, after he became a Sadducee, until the time of the victory there was no Nasi and no Av Beit Din from among the Pharisees, and so the last Nasi was Joshua ben Peraḥiah. If so, of whom is it fitting to say "my husband dwells with you"? This is without doubt aimed at the Nasi who is in Alexandria, and who was this Nasi if not Joshua ben Peraḥiah? Now it is proved that it was Joshua who returned because of Simeon's call, and certainly he returned to be Nasi as he had been before, and then Simeon was Av Beit Din. Afterward, when Yannai persecuted the Pharisees, many sages also fled to Alexandria, and it was a time of distress for the Pharisees until Yannai died; and perhaps during these days of distress Joshua died, for he was already old and advanced in years. After Yannai's death Simeon was Nasi and Judah ben Tabbai Av Beit Din. So, according to my conjecture, were the matters. And from this arose the difference of opinions among the later [authorities]. For it was received among them that Simeon was Av Beit Din, but they erred and thought that this was when Judah ben Tabbai was his colleague, and from this was born the mistaken reading that Judah ben Tabbai was Nasi. Likewise, since they knew that in the days of Yannai sages fled to Alexandria, as Josephus tells, they thought that Judah ben Tabbai was among those who fled; and believing that Judah was Simeon's colleague, they thought that the letter Simeon wrote was aimed at Judah; and from this arose the error in the Yerushalmi.
